chunks: "Generally I avoid them on the fastest and most sensitive nets, or I design special ones, because a test point isn't free electrically.
On a fast net, the pad is a bit of capacitance, around half a picofarad with its stub, hanging off a 50 ohm line.
With a 100 picosecond edge that reflects around 12 percent of the step, and the stub can resonate, which closes the eye on a multi-gigabit link.
On a sensitive analog or reference net, the pad and the probe load it, add leakage and pick up noise, so the thing you measure isn't what the circuit does.

So for high-speed nets I'd use an in-line pad where the trace itself passes over the pad so there's no stub, or a very short stub with an isolation resistor right at the tap, or an RF connector or footprint I can populate for validation, and rely on built-in eye scan or margining and measure at the receiver or connector.
For sensitive analog nets I'd add a buffered test output, a guarded point, or skip it and read the value through the ADC or a status register.
If I must have a pad in bring-up, I'd place it, measure, and remove it in production if it affects margin.
And I'd put it at the point that gives the most information, usually the receiver end."
